newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Russia not seen making De Beers ultimatum.
newsitem.headline: Russia not seen making De Beers ultimatum.

text.p: De Beers' demand that Russia sign a new diamond deal by the end of the year is unlikely to be met by the Russians who have been dragging their feet for the past ten months, analysts and dealers said on Wednesday.

De Beers' announcement that from December 31 it would no longer buy Russian diamonds under an old marketing agreement was interpreted by commentators as a move to force Russian authorities to ratify a new agreement, on hold since February.

"De Beers has indicated to the Russian Government and ARS (producer Almazy Rossii-Sakha) that it is not prepared to continue to buy diamonds under the old agreement beyond 31 December 1996," the diamond giant said in a statement.
While dealers and analysts said they did not believe Russia would secede from the De Beers empire, like Australian producer Argyle, they said an agreement by the end of the year was unlikely.
"Possibly not within the next 12 days. It's too short a time," Des Mayer, analyst at G O'Flaherty told Reuters.
Still commentators did not believe that the move would sour Russian/De Beers relations to the point of no return.

They said that the two parties were likely to continue more or less the way they had been since February, when a memorandum of understanding for a new deal was signed, but that this latest development would bring matters to a head.

"It was inevitable that this type of thing was going to happen. De Beers has been strung on for quite some time now. Co-operation will continue and there will be an agreement at some stage. This (the ultimatum) will heighten the urgency of sorting out the problems," Mayers said.

Dealers said that while the De Beers share sank after the Russian news, it remained underpinned by sound fundamentals -- not least of all the $4.834 billion made from rough diamond sales through the CSO compared with $4.531 billion previously.

"The shares are being sold on the back of the Russian news. There are a lot of small sellers. But there are also a lot of buying orders and the share should remain underpinned by the record sales," one dealer said.

Last year De Beers, whose London-based Central Selling Organisation (CSO) accounts for some 75 percent of global diamond sales, was knocked by sales of renegade Russian stones directly onto the world market.
Analysts say that the CSO ensures market stability for a commodity whose value is not utility-based.
De Beers has spent 1996 trying to secure a new marketing deal with Russia without success as that country has endured political turmoil which has overshadowed any diamond deal.
Commentators said that Russia would lose without an agreement and that the ultimatum might concentrate the minds of the Russain authorities.
"There are so many personalities involved, protecting their own position. This may put a cat among the pigeons there," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
